parts.problem_md:
A student investigates the reaction between metal **F** and dilute sulfuric acid.

**(i) Procedure**

The student:

- adds 3 cm depth of dilute sulfuric acid to a test-tube
- adds a spatula of metal F to the test-tube
- observes the mixture fizzing slowly
- tests the gas produced with a lighted splint
- hears a squeaky pop.

Identify the gas produced.

[1]

(ii) The student repeats the procedure from (a)(i) but also adds aqueous copper(II) sulfate to the dilute sulfuric acid and metal F.

The student observes that this reaction is faster than the reaction in (a)(i).

Suggest **one** observation the student makes which shows that this reaction is faster.

[1]

(iii)

**Procedure**

The student:

- pours a small volume of the aqueous product from the procedure in (a)(i) into a test‑tube
- adds aqueous sodium hydroxide
- observes a white precipitate.

Use this observation to suggest **two** possible identities for the cation produced from metal F.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (i) Hydrogen, H<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) Fizzes more / solid disappears more quickly **[1 mark]**
> - (iii) Zinc (Zn<sup>2+</sup>) or calcium (Ca<sup>2+</sup>) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept a quicker rate of bubbles / more effervescence

> **[exam-tip]**
> A white precipitate with sodium hydroxide doesn't distinguish between Zn<sup>2+</sup> and Ca<sup>2+</sup> on its own — you'd need an extra test (excess NaOH dissolves the zinc precipitate but not the calcium one) to tell them apart, which is why both are accepted here.

parts.problem_md:
You are going to investigate the reaction between metal **F** and dilute sulfuric acid.

**(a) Procedure:**

- Add 3 cm depth of dilute sulfuric acid to a clean test-tube.
- Add a spatula of metal F to the test-tube.
- Test the gas produced in the reaction to identify it.

(i) State the test used to identify the gas and give the observation for a positive result.

[1]

(ii) State the name of the gas.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Test: lighted splint; observation: squeaky pop **[1 mark]**
> - Gas: hydrogen **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept H<sub>2</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The "squeaky pop" test is unique to hydrogen — no other common gas gives this exact result with a lighted splint.

parts.problem_md:
Iron(II) ions, Fe<sup>2+</sup>, are formed from atoms of iron, Fe.

(i) Describe how Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions are formed from iron atoms.

[1]

(ii) Describe what is observed when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to aqueous iron(II) ions.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (i) The atom loses two electrons **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) Green **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) A precipitate is formed **[1 mark]**
> 
> Ignore any reference to turning brown

> **[exam-tip]**
> Iron(II) hydroxide precipitate is green and can slowly turn brown on standing in air — but this question only asks about the immediate observation.
